  • Get the list of all devices that need to be computed.
  • While the list is not empty, pull one element and do the computation

So I mentioned the radio because it is the simplest real life application of a contiguous analog system. (Contiguous as opposed to discrete and analog as opposed to digital.)

The real difference is that the whole system works as a whole and can do complex things like integration differentiation or filtering in realtime. Simulating such a behavior in the digital domain has always been slow and prone to errors. Our paradigm of ordered execution is simply not suitable.

What I'm driving at is that the examples of intelligence in nature are all analog and contiguous, so it is unlikely that we can replicate them using fully digital systems. We will probably need some sort of hybrid approach. In AI research and CS in general the understanding of the analog domain is almost completely lacking and this causes a certain blindness and lack of imagination.

So I advise you to obtain at least a rudimentary understanding of analog electronics, and pay special attention to 'time domain analysis' and 'frequency domain analysis'. These are two extraordinarily powerful techniques for looking at and analyzing problems. There is no need to go all mathy and theoretical about them, just learn how to use an oscilloscope and a spectrum analyzer. Two pieces of equipment that will add two new dimensions to your understanding of complex phenomena.

Most likely your way of looking at problems will never be the same again.

Human's neural nets have been operating and training for their entire life. They have already learned how to focus and ignore data before they ever learn what an apple even is. So when you train a network, you have to train it with data that will allow it to filter out the noise as well as recognize the apple. However humans already learned that just by being born. The sheer amount of data that people take in on a daily basis dwarfs the amount of data it takes to train an ANN. An infant can't make the visual connections as easily as you say, although they should be able to do it with fewer examples than an ANN simply due to a more evolved network structure. That doesn't mean that the current ANN's aren't "intelligent". It's a difference in expectations. Maybe in 200 years we will have the computing power to build massive networks that can mimic the efficiency and intuition that humans take for granted. But for now, we are essentially in the stone age of ANN research. Most of the big 'discoveries' (aside from AlphaGo) are about network structure that are painfully obvious after the fact. There are a lot more problems to be solved with NN's. NN's are legit, proved by AlphaGo. I'm sure the hype will die out soon, but what is left is a serious contender for machine learning implementations now that we are closing in on the computing power to run network calcs in a reasonable time.

Power will help, but the training algorithms NN use are inherently dumb. Stochastic Gradient Descent is the issue. It just attempts to go down the error curve. Thats why it needs so many examples. And it will need exponentially more examples as you bump up the power because the amount of free variables skyrockets. There are so many parameters to update, in the order of millions for current 5 layer networks.

Deep Learning helped by greedily training the layers using auto-encoding or RBMs, but i wouldn't say its the end game. Deep Learning just trains the weights a chunk at a time, so that we don't have to worry about all the free parameters at once. Look up the vanishing gradient problem. This is what deep nets solve.
